expected_evidence: Geological: a continent-wide platinum/iridium enrichment layer at the Younger Dryas boundary (~12,800-12,900 cal BP) in sediment cores, ice cores, and paleosols across North America (this layer is independently well-documented, e.g., Greenland ice core Pt spike, Moore et al. continental Pt anomaly)

Astronomical/geological: a diagnostic radioisotope signature (notably live 60Fe, or anomalous isotopic ratios inconsistent with chondritic/asteroidal material) in the same stratigraphic horizon, since supernova ejecta carries a distinct nucleosynthetic fingerprint different from solar-system impactor material
Astronomical: identification of a supernova remnant or compact stellar remnant with a kinematic age and distance consistent with reaching Earth ~10,850 BCE
Geological: nanodiamonds, magnetic spherules, and other impact-proxy markers co-located with the platinum spike, and their isotopic composition tested against supernova vs. asteroidal origin
Material/archaeological: disruption horizon in Clovis-era sites correlated with the anomaly layer
Genetic: megafauna extinction/bottleneck signatures dated to the same interval

Model-prior (theoretical): physical plausibility of a nearby supernova depositing a sharp, localized 'fallout' pulse of platinum-group elements rather than a diffuse, long-duration interstellar dust increase
response.rationale: The hypothesis maps to the Younger Dryas boundary interval (~10,850 BCE ≈ 12,800-12,900 cal BP) and proposes a supernova, rather than an asteroid/comet, as the source of the well-known North American platinum anomaly. Using the younger-dryas detectability rows, the most relevant evidence classes are geological (0.65) and astronomical (0.7), both comparatively high — this class of evidence is exactly the kind (ice cores, sediment layers, isotopic fingerprints) that has demonstrably survived and been recovered for this period, since the platinum/iridium boundary layer itself is already an established empirical finding in the literature (model-prior: Greenland ice-core Pt spike, Moore et al. 2017 continental Pt anomaly, nanodiamond/spherule studies). Because detectability for the diagnostic evidence types is moderate-to-high rather than low, an absence of corroborating supernova-specific signals (e.g., live 60Fe or non-chondritic isotopic ratios, or a remnant of matching age/distance) is more likely attributable to the mechanism being incorrect than to poor preservation or search effort. Model-prior astrophysics also weighs against plausibility: known nearby-supernova radioisotope events (e.g., ~2-3 Myr ago from the Local Bubble, and the ~65 kyr and ~2 Myr deep-sea 60Fe detections) show that such events leave a distinct, well-preserved isotopic signature quite different from a localized 'impact ejecta fallout' pulse of platinum-group elements — the latter morphology is the consensus signature of an extraterrestrial (asteroidal/cometary) impactor, not diffuse supernova dust. I therefore set the detectability_adjustment modestly below the raw table average for the compound evidence needed (geological+astronomical+model_prior), reflecting that while detection was plausible and evidence-recovery infrastructure exists, the specific corroborating supernova signature has not been reported despite active, ongoing search in this exact stratigraphic context — an absence that argues against, not merely obscures, the hypothesis. This assessment leans on model-prior knowledge of supernova nucleosynthesis/radioisotope signatures and existing Younger Dryas Pt/Ir literature, which should be treated as an unverified, low-tier source pending direct evidence-text confirmation.
